title: Throughput benchmarking harness and methodology (wip)
content:
Purpose:
This doc describes the throughput benchmarking harness and recommended methodology for the serving runtime team. It focuses on load generator configs, warmup and steady-state detection, repeatability, and profiling hooks so that we produce stable, comparable numbers across hardware, model variants, and runtime changes.

Scope and goals:
- Provide a repeatable harness and measurement approach for peak and sustained throughput (tokens/sec and requests/sec).
- Minimize measurement noise due to client-side bottlenecks, networking, and cold-start effects.
- Standardize load generator configs and templates for common workload shapes (chat, completion, embeddings).
- Define warmup and steady-state criteria and a statistical approach to reporting.
- Instrument hooks for low-overhead profiling to identify bottlenecks (CPU, GPU utilization, memory, kernel hotspots).

Benchmarking harness architecture (high level):
- Coordinator (bench controller): orchestrates experiments, collects metrics, and stores metadata for each run.
- Load generator instances: multiple hosts or containers that drive traffic to the target serving cluster. We prefer dedicated worker VMs to avoid client CPU contention.
- Metric collectors: Prometheus exporters on serving instances, NVML exporters for GPU metrics, and client-side telemetry.
- Result aggregator: collates time series and produces summary CSVs and plots.
- Experiment metadata store: save config, git commit, model version, quantization profile, and random seeds.

Load generator best practices:
- Use multiple client workers distributed across at least 2 AZs to avoid single-host networking saturation.
- Drive synthetic requests with realistic sequence-length distributions and batch sizes that mirror production.
- Prefer asynchronous clients that can issue multiple outstanding requests per connection; tune to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- Ensure client machines have headroom (CPU and network) so they're not the bottleneck. Monitor client-side CPU, p99 latency, and NIC stats.
- Use TLS and auth as in production when measuring end-to-end, but also run an intra-cluster measurement (no TLS) to isolate serving runtime performance.

Load profiles and config templates (concepts):
- Workload shape: chat-like (many short prefix tokens, small incremental outputs), completion-like (single request with long output), embedding (fixed input size, CPU-bound tokenizers).
- Key params: concurrency (number of outstanding requests per worker), qps target, request batch size, request token lengths (input and expected output), sampling strategy for sequence lengths.
- Example fields in a loadgen config (YAML):
  - model: name/version
  - deploy_url: endpoint
  - workers: 8
  - concurrency_per_worker: 16
  - batch_size: 1 or up to model's optimum
  - seq_len_input_distribution: distribution name or histogram file
  - expected_output_tokens: 32
  - sampling_seed: 42
  - request_timeout_sec: 60
  - use_streaming: true|false

Sequence length distributions and sampling:
- Capture production token length histograms for major routes and use them to synthesize load. Use a seed to ensure deterministic sampling.
- For peak throughput tests, use the 95th percentile combined seq_len (input+output) or synthetic fixed lengths to stress the runtime. For cost/efficiency tests use median lengths.

Warmup protocol and steady-state detection:
- Problem: GPU kernels, cuBLAS, and caching layers (KV caches, memory allocators) have varying latency on cold runs. We need a deterministic warmup policy so runs are comparable.
- Recommended warmup sequence:
  1) Start serving cluster and verify all nodes healthy.
  2) Run a deterministic micro-benchmark (single-threaded short seqs) to initialize CUDA context and kernels.
  3) Run an adaptive warmup load: issue traffic at increasing concurrency ramps until observed throughput stabilizes. Typical pattern: 30s @ low qps -> 2m ramp to target qps -> 5m at target qps.
  4) Consider an additional cache-warming pass using representative prompts covering the model's tokenizer spectrum.
- Steady-state criteria: require at least 3 contiguous minutes where 1-min throughput variance < 3% and p99 latency < threshold. Only collect measurement windows after steady-state is reached.

Measurement windows and reporting:
- Run at least N=5 independent trials per configuration; each trial should have a warmup phase and a measurement phase (measurement window >= 5 minutes).
- Report mean and 95% confidence interval for throughput and latency percentiles (p50, p90, p95, p99). Provide the raw time-series CSV for auditability.
- Report system metrics averaged over the measurement window: GPU utilization, GPU memory usage, CPU usage, PCIe throughput, PCIe retries, host network Tx/Rx, context-switches.
- Tag results with metadata: git commit, model id, quantization info, instance type, driver/CUDA version, NVML snapshot.

Statistical considerations and repeatability:
- Use deterministic seeds for sampled prompts and sampling randomness whenever possible. Record seeds in metadata.
- When comparing variants (e.g., quantized vs fp16), always run interleaved trials (rotate order of runs) to avoid time-of-day or cluster-load confounds.
- Use bootstrap or t-test for statistical significance between runs; avoid over-interpreting isolated p99 differences.

Profiling hooks and low-overhead instrumentation:
- Lightweight profiling (production safe): aggregate GPU SM utilization, active kernel names (sampled), nvprof/Nsys summaries on a subset of runs.
- Detailed profiling: for targeted experiments use Nsight or nsys capture for a single node with a short, deterministic workload. Capture timeline with CPU/GPU correlation.
- Tracing: enable request-level tracing (trace-id) for sampled requests to inspect queuing and per-request timings (enqueue, dequeue, model-run-start, model-run-end, postprocess).
- Expose internal counters from runtime: batch sizes observed, queue lengths, cache hit rates, kernel launch latencies.

Common pitfalls and mitigations:
- Client-side bottleneck: CPU-saturated load generator leads to under-reporting throughput. Mitigate by adding workers or using faster clients.
- Network saturation: use multiple AZs and measure NIC util.
- Warmup insufficient: ignore first 2-3 minutes if warmup incomplete.
- Non-deterministic tokenization: canonicalize tokenization pipeline and version tokenizer artifacts.
- Hidden autoscaling or scheduling interference: pin serving nodes and disable autoscaling during a benchmark.

Example commands and samples (appendix):
- Quick run (single node): ./benchctl run --config configs/bert-like-256.yml --trials 5 --measurement 300
- YAML example (short):
  model: gptx-small-v1
  endpoint: https://cluster.internal/models/gptx-small-v1
  workers: 6
  concurrency_per_worker: 8
  batch_size: 4
  seq_len_input_distribution: data/prod_histogram_chat.json
  expected_output_tokens: 64
  warmup: {ramp_seconds: 120, steady_seconds: 180}

- Output artifacts: each trial produces a results/ folder with:
  - metrics.csv (timestamped per-second throughput/latency)
  - system-metrics.prom.json (prom scrape)
  - profile.nsys (optional detailed capture)
  - metadata.json (git commit, config, seeds)

Next steps and action items:
- (Meera) Add sample histograms for chat/completion/embeddings in data/ and add a script to convert production traces into histograms. Due: 2024-09-10.
- (Tomás) Integrate NVML exporter into benchctl and ensure driver/version tagging. Due: 2024-09-05.
- (Aisha) Run a 3-model sweep (fp16, q4f16, q8_0) on p4 vs a100 and report comparative throughput/latency. Due: 2024-09-20.

Notes and rationale (short):
- We favor longer measurement windows and repeated trials to reduce variance introduced by kernel JIT, GC, or cluster noise.
- Warmup should aim to exercise the same codepaths as measurement traffic so runtime caches and memory pools are warmed.
- Recording raw artifacts (CSV, traces, profile captures) is critical for post-hoc analysis; summary numbers alone are not sufficient.

Appendix: minimal CSV columns expected in metrics.csv:
- timestamp_iso, requests_per_sec, tokens_per_sec, p50_ms, p90_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, gpu_util_percent, gpu_mem_mb, cpu_percent

References and prior docs:
- throughput-benchmarking-harness-and-methodology.json (baseline)
- throughput-benchmarking-harness-and-methodology-wip.json (earlier draft)
- throughput-benchmarking-harness-and-methodology-notes.json

Feedback welcome: please add comments inline or ping #eng-serving-runtime with experimental results and sample artifacts for catalogue.
